Thank you, Madam Chair, Excellencies. I am honored to present an oral report on the Committee's work during 2025 and to share both the challenges and the hopes in advancing the full realization of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. This year, the Committee held its 32nd and 33rd session in Geneva amid the severe liquidity crisis affecting the United Nations. Despite this constrict, the Committee continued to fulfill its mandate with professionalism and commitment, reviewing reports, adopting list of issues, and consideration communication to uphold the rights of persons with disabilities. However, meeting time was reduced to 12 working days instead of 20, and the committee was unable to review all scheduled reports. More than 13 state parties have yet to undergo their first review, contributing to backlog of 54 reports representing a delay of nearly five years. We therefore urge the General Assembly to ensure stable and predictable funding for all treaty bodies, because human rights cannot depend on financial convenience. Furthermore, many members of the Committee themselves are persons with disabilities, continue to face barriers due to the lack of reasonable accommodation during meetings. Accessibility is not a privilege, but a human right. The Committee deeply regret that national sign language interpretation for deaf members was not provided fully during the two sessions this year and has been excluded from the official UN budget. This decision contradicts the Secretary-General's disability inclusion strategy and undermines the principle of accessibility that the United Nations itself must uphold. True inclusion must begin with the UN so that it may credibly lead by example. Despite this, the Committee continued its substantive work with determination, including the drafting of a general comment on Article 11, situation of risk and humanitarian emergencies, and Article 29, participation in political and public life. In this time of growing instability and humanitarian crisis, persons with disabilities face heightened threat to their safety and dignity. Our work on Article 11 with the General Comment is particularly significant as it seeks to strengthen protection and inclusion in context of crisis, including armed conflict, natural disasters and public health emergencies. During the 33rd session, the Committee held an open dialogue in Geneva with persons with disabilities from conflict-affected regions such as Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem, together with UN agencies and State Parties. Participants shared moving testimonies of how people with disabilities are too often left behind during evacuations, rescue lists, and deprive medical care, assistive devices, and rehabilitation services. Each conflict not only destroys infrastructure, but also creates new disabilities and deep psychological trauma. From the Committee's perspective, war itself has become a disability issue, creating new impairments, defending exclusion, and denying dignity to those most at risk. The Committee welcomes recent ceasefire efforts and expresses hope that they will mark a turning point towards peace and inclusive recovery. We call upon all parties, humanitarian actors and donors to ensure that disability inclusion is At the core of reconstruction, through accessible infrastructure, rehabilitation, psychosocial support, and the meaningful participation of organizations of persons with disabilities. Persons with disabilities are already among the world's poorest population, are being pushed into even deeper poverty than ever before amid war, climate crisis, natural disasters and global economic recession. At this crucial moment, the international community has demonstrated renewed solidarity through the Amman-Berlin Declaration adopted last April in Berlin and endorsed by over 90 State Parties to the CRPD. together with United Nations agencies and organizations of persons with disabilities. The Committee warmly welcomed this declaration which represents an inspiring commitment under Article 32 of the Convention on international cooperation reaffirming that global partnership is essential to advancing the rights and inclusion of persons with disabilities. As we approach next year, 2026, marking the 20th anniversary of the Convention, its transformative legacy is evident. The CRPD redefined human rights by recognizing intersectional discrimination and embedding equality and dignity for all humanity. Let this anniversary be not a reflection on unfulfilled promise, but a renewed commitment to ensure that no one is left behind because of disability. I call on all member states to let us by the convention, strengthening support through the General Assembly and joining in shaping a shared vision for the next 20 years, a plan of hope for 1.3 billion persons with disability around the world and their families. With 193 state already parties, we look forward to those not yet among them, including the United States, Palau, Kiribati, Tonga and the Holy See, so that no country stands apart from this shared journey. Together, let us ensure that through the rights of persons with disabilities, humanity itself moves closer to the full realization of human rights. I thank you so much.

Thank you. Chairpersons, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I am honored to engage in this interactive dialogue for the second time since assuming the mandate of the Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2023. This has been a remarkable year for persons with disabilities. The third global disability summit in April brought together nearly 5,000 participants from 160 countries. At the summit, 74 governments endorsed the Berlin Amman Declaration, committing to advance the full implementation of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and promoting disability inclusive international development cooperation and humanitarian action. In 2026, we will mark the 20th anniversary of the Convention, an opportunity to take stock and reaffirm to the full realization of the rights of persons with disabilities. In 20 years, the Convention has achieved near universal ratification. These milestones highlight broad support, but also undermine the urgent need for concrete action and funding. Excellencies, I am deeply concerned by finding cuts in international development and humanitarian action, which affects the rights-based advocacy, service delivery, and the functioning of many organizations of persons with disabilities. Their voices are essential in identifying barriers and ensuring meaningful participation in policymaking. The funding crisis has also impacted on my mandate and on other UN human rights mechanisms, and it has reduced the UN capacity for disability mainstreaming inclusion and operation, including in peace, security and humanitarian response. And at the national level, we see cases of regression in social security and support services for persons with disabilities. Distinguished delegates, these trends have direct impact on individuals and communities. In the report I am presenting today to the Third Committee, I highlight the barriers that children with disabilities and their families face in enjoying their human rights. Everywhere in the world, families have been expected to shoulder care and support needs of children with disabilities in absence of adequate public infrastructure services. Frequently, the only alternative they were offered are residential institutions and therefore separation. Children with disabilities have the right to grow up in a family, access mainstream education and receive support services, including healthcare, transport, sports, culture, individualized support, assistive devices, and rehabilitation. However, the extra cost linked to raising a child with a disability are mostly carried by families. In some countries, these extra costs surpass the national average income. Moreover, family caregivers face discrimination by association with the person of disability, which is a form of disability-based discrimination. This creates barriers, for example, to gain and mainstream employment, pension rights, and be included and welcome in public spaces. The cycle of poverty and exclusion is thus reinforced. A significant gender dimension exists as it is largely women, especially mothers, who assume the role of the primary caregivers. Due to the persistence of gender stereotypes, ideal of motherhood and ableist attitude, women are often expected to give their time, economic independence and social lives to provide unpaid care for a child with a disability with minimal support except for pity and glorification of their self-sacrifice. But pity and admiration alone do not provide financial stability, health and inclusion for mothers and children. My report details promising practices and concrete recommendations on right-based support to family caregivers and children with disabilities. Holistic, integrated and inclusive approaches are needed to ensure children growing in stable, healthy family environment. This gives them the best chance for lifelong inclusion and empowers independent living in the community. Excellencies. Caregivers and children with disabilities have too often been overlooked in our laws and policies. As we move towards inclusive, human rights-based care and support systems, we have the opportunity to ensure that every child with a disability enjoys the right to a family life, support and responsive and equitable policies. This is also a crucial step towards preventing institutionalization and recognizing the vital, often unpaid care work carried largely by women. I urge member states to consider these recommendations when developing and implementing national policies and strategies on care and support. These frameworks provide key opportunities to address the needs of both those providing and requiring care and support. Family caregivers and children with disabilities are uniquely positioned to contribute to both perspectives. Thank you all.

Madam Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, and esteemed participants. It is my privilege to present you my thematic report entitled "Minority Issues in the Context of the UN Reform Process." Let me be clear that the reform process I am referring to is not only the UN at 80 exercise, but a much more fundamental reset of the multilateral system prompted by a series of seismic evolution on the world stage in the past few years. In that context, 2025 is one of special significance for the protection of human rights in the United Nations, as attacks on the human rights system have never been so violent. A revealing and shocking example is the USA deliberately and openly violating its international obligations. In that respect, I unconditionally denounce the US government's sanction on the Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory. I express my full solidarity with Francesca Albanese. Sanctioning a Special Rapporteur appointed by the Human Rights Council violates international law and is a direct attack on the integrity of the UN human rights system, including UN special procedures as a whole. I call on all States to act decisively to denounce these sanctions and refuse to carry them out. I also call on the United States of America to immediately withdraw these illegal measures. These attacks by the US, as well as blatant disregard for the most basic human rights by several other governments, call for a major upheaval of the very foundation of the multilateral system, including its backbone, that is the United Nations. Such processes may be an opportunity for minority issues to be given a better consideration in the future reconfigured multilateral system. I am encouraged in this prospect by the constructive relationship my mandate has been building with key actors dealing with minority issues as diverse as Chile, China, the EU and its member states, and particularly Austria and Hungary, Iraq, Nepal, Pakistan and Somalia. I hope these existing constructive dialogues will lead to concrete results for the benefit of persons belonging to minorities in the near future. Because the truth is that minority issues have never really found a place in the United Nations system. When adopting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948, the General Assembly acknowledged that, I quote, "The United Nations cannot remain indifferent to the fate of minorities, but considering the universal character of the Declaration of Human Rights, it decided not to deal in a specific provision with the question of minorities in the text of the declaration." Madam Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, and esteemed participants, minorities are misfits in the United Nations system for the protection of human rights. Interestingly, the original regime of minority protection prior to international human rights law under the League of Nations had more to do with peace and security issues than with human rights. One of the needed change of perspective regarding minority issues in the new multilateral system is that they should not remain confined to the margin of the human rights pillar, but should also be addressed as peace and security issue. In 2022, commemorating the 30 years of having adopted the Declaration on the Right of Persons Belonging to Minorities, the Secretary-General addressing the General Assembly concluded that the declaration, I quote, "enshrined three core truths. First, that minority rights are human rights. Second, that the protection of minorities is integral to the mission of the United Nations. Third, that the promotion of those rights is vital to advancing political and social stability and preventing conflict within and between countries. In that perspective, the research conducted to draft the present report showed that since 1948, 78 Security Council resolutions have addressed minority issues two of them adopted last year. Coming back to the 2022 speech, the Secretary General, Gutierrez, also spoke harsh word on the effective implementation of this 92 declaration. He said, I quote, the hard truth is that 30 years on, the world is failing short, far short. We're not dealing with gaps, we are dealing with outright inaction and negligence in the protection of minority rights. The extensive research I led with the help of young dedicated university students, show that the situation is not as bleak as it appears. My report shows that there are quite many United Nations entities, funds, programs, specialist agencies, and related organizations that positively impact the lives of persons belonging to minorities through their activities. The problem is that these actions are not visible because they are often not labeled as explicitly dealing with minorities. In many instances, actions are conflated with issues that concern other marginalized groups, such as indigenous people, people experiencing racism, or vulnerable groups. So the problem is invisibility of the action, not a lack of action. And this is rather good news, because this existing action can be made visible without a major budgetary increase. but it will need some political will. This is why, in the conclusion of this opening remark, I call on Member States. First, I call on Member States to continue supporting existing minority-focused UN activities, such as the UN Forum on Minority Issues, the Minority Fellowship Programme, the Faith for Rights framework, as well as the UN Network on Racial Discrimination and Protection of Minorities. Second, In order to better integrate concern and the rights of persons belonging to minorities into a renewed UN architecture, I ask member states through the General Assembly's Sixth Committee to request the International Law Commission in the context of the progressive development of international law and in accordance with Article 16 of its statute to include in its program of work the issue of the protection of minorities and persons belonging to minorities. And third, and last but not least, I ask States to acknowledge the regrettable invisibility of minority issues as illustrated by the absence of even a single mention of minorities in the Sustainable Development Goals or in the recent Pact for the Future. In order to close this gap and to raise the importance of minority issues within the UN, making certain that minorities are adequately reflected and engaged with in the post-2030 agenda, I call for the UN to organize a world summit on minority issues in the perspective of the post-2030 agenda. Let me remind you that minority issues are closely linked to a renewed multilateral system able to guarantee peace and stability, justice and well-being for all without anyone being left behind because they belong to a minority. Minority issues are core to effective multilateralism. Historical and recent events have shown the dramatic consequences when such issues are left to be dealt with bilaterally by neighboring states. Thank you.

Madam Chair, we align ourselves with the statement made by the European Union. We welcome the Special Rapporteur on Minority Issues, Mr. Nicolas Loeb, to the Third Committee and express our appreciation for his comprehensive and wide-ranging activities, as well as his report on minority issues in the context of the United Nations reform process. The 20th century has taught us to pay better attention to the importance of minority affairs and that the recognition of their identity and the full enjoyment of their human rights without discrimination contributes to peace and prosperity all over the world. It is the more regrettable that minority issues have never really found their place in the United Nations system. We agree with the Special Rapporteur that we have to take it seriously and make concrete steps to change the fact that persons belonging to national or ethnic, religious and linguistic minorities are the last major group at the UN with no specific mechanism or initiative to strengthen the protection of their human rights. It is high time that the Member States step up to protect minorities and make the commitments taken in the Declaration on the Rights of Persons Belonging to National or Ethnic, Religious and Linguistic Minorities a reality for minorities everywhere. The reform of the multilateral system presents an opportunity to rethink and revitalize the proper approach to minority issues within the framework of a transforming UN. This opportunity must also be seized to condemn and identify effective actions against the persecution and discrimination faced by religious minorities. Thank you, Madam Chair. And first, let me thank all the States who took the floor and expressed support for the general vision that I propose in this report. I hear the support for a number of states and also coming from different geographical and geopolitical region to find ways to improve the manner in which the United Nations deals with minority issue. I inform state representatives that next year report to the Human Rights Committee, Geneva, not here, will be trying to figure out what are minority issues, because the mandate is not only on minority rights, but is on minority issue. And I think it is important to identify these type of issues, which are different in different part of the world, in different socioeconomic situation, in different geopolitical relationship. So hoping that more states will feel concern by the way minorities and minority issues are dealt with in their country and in the United Nations. Second point, I think we've heard several intervening states making specific remarks about the situation of human groups which are minority in neighboring countries and how this is a preoccupation. And yes, it is a preoccupation, both as regards the violation of human rights and as regards the potential for tension in international relation between neighboring states. This is why, and I heard several of the intervening states express their appreciation of the concept that it is not only through the lens of human rights, but also as a matter of good neighborhood relation and peace and security within national society and between national societies. So, naturally, if I had a very good idea and a very good solution on how to improve things, I wouldn't hide it from you, it would have been in my report, it's not yet there. But I appreciate the willingness to enter into the matter and to work together, hopefully, to increase awareness and improve existing mechanisms. As was said, the minorities themselves as a specific category or a specific large group do not have any specific UN mechanism dedicated to their protection. I am not sure we need to reinvent something because, as my report has shown, there are many things being done. It's just that they have to be put together in a proper way, in a proper order. I'm very conscious of the difficulties financial difficulties of the multilateral system, and I'm not necessarily asking for solution which will be costly, but we have to find way to better use existing mechanism. I heard a question from the representative of the EU about how to improve the functioning and the output of the minority forum. I was very pleased to hear from Austria that several of the recommendations that came out of the forum made it through the resolution that will be tabled and, I hope, adopted on the mandate. This is one specificity of the mandate, but it is true that the forum is more an agora, a place where representatives of different discriminated groups come to present the case and the complaints than a place for constructive discussion. I'm trying to find ways to make it more constructive, but I must say that the demands from civil society organization and states are hard to make work together, especially in a two-day event. But be assured that I'm working to make it more efficient more constructive, even though it is also needed to have a space for civil society to express its grief. I was asked how it is possible to increase visibility of minorities within UN activities. Well, one of the difficulty with this invisibilization of action in favor of minority groups is linked to the fact that very often the initial assessment of the situation identifies these groups that are being discriminated, but in many cases, for political reasons, very often domestic political reasons, there's a reluctance of states to enter into this minority language. Again, I am trained as an academic, a researcher, so I'm trying to understand where this reluctance comes from and how we can circumvent it, both in the action of the different UN program and organization at national level and within the multilateral system. Certainly, a way to increase visibility is to increase diversity in representation from member states, Most states are diverse. It was said by several of those who intervened, are diverse in language, in confessions, in cultural practices, and naturally, I think it's also maybe not here in the third committee, but in many UN activities, a possibility to portray this national diversity through representation through the UN. And last point, Actually, there are many others, but I hope we can cooperate in the coming years. How to strengthen minority protection to guarantee sustainable peace? Actually, I think this term of sustainable peace is very relevant, very important. Peace is not only the absence of conflict or war. This is a situation in which different components of society can work together to develop and to enhance the well-being of all members of society, including persons belonging to minorities. So, again, solutions are not yet fully baked. We need to work on it. I am launching a series of consultations, and I really count on the input from different states, be it through their national representation in multilateral fora, be it through supporting academic program of research on minority issues. And actually, the last proposal that I make in my report is to reflect and try to find whether it is possible to develop an index which would allow to appreciate how the situation of minority in each context is either improving or degrading. Again, as an academic, I have been very critical to many composite index which do not reflect reality, but on the other hand, it gives us a tool to assess the dynamic of the situation. So, yes, it is work in progress. Thank you once again very much for the support I heard from all the intervening states. And I will take the silence of the others as, as we say in French, "qui ne dit mot consent", acceptance that work needs to be undertook and to be progressively included in the different pillars of the UN system. Thank you, Madam Chair.
